posts.title: "Mimi Ndyo Edwin Sifuna"
posts.excerpt: The air inside the Orange Democratic Movement headquarters hung thick with the weight of history and betrayal. Edwin Watenya Sifuna, the man who had served as the party's Secretary General since 2018, the articulate firebrand who had defended the party's ideals with the precision of a surgeon and the passion of a revolutionary, walked out of those doors for the last time as an ODM insider.
posts.content:
For eight years, Sifuna had been the voice of the party, the legal mind who could dismantle an opponent's argument in one breath and rally a crowd in the next. He had steered the party through turbulent waters, delivered Nairobi County to ODM in the 2022 General Election with an overwhelming mandate, and stood shoulder-to-shoulder with Raila Odinga, the doyen of Kenyan opposition politics. But politics, like law, is ultimately about interpretation and Sifuna could no longer reconcile his interpretation of the opposition's future with the direction the party was taking.

The rift was not personal; it was existential. Raila Odinga's political directions and alliances had shifted the tectonic plates beneath the opposition, and Sifuna, ever the advocate for the people, found himself on the wrong side of a movement he had helped build. When the dust settled, the Secretary General was no more. But from the ashes of that departure, something remarkable began to rise.

From the Halls of Nairobi to the Heart of the City

To understand Edwin Sifuna's ascent, one must first understand the foundation. A law graduate from the University of Nairobi's Class of 2006, Sifuna cut his teeth in the rigorous corridors of legal academia before being admitted to the Roll of Advocates in 2008. As a partner at E. Sifuna & Associates Advocates, he built a reputation not merely as a lawyer, but as a defender of the public interest, a thread that would run through his entire political career.
The law gave him language. It taught him to argue, to persuade, to dismantle power structures with evidence and rhetoric. But Nairobi gave him his stage. When he ran for Senator of Nairobi County in 2022 under the ODM banner, he did not merely campaign, he connected. The city, with its sprawling informal settlements, its ambitious middle class, and its restless youth, saw in Sifuna something different: a politician who could speak the language of the courtroom and the street with equal fluency.
He won overwhelmingly. And in that victory, the seeds of something larger were planted.

Linda Mwananchi: The Movement Takes Root

After his exit from ODM leadership, Sifuna did not retreat. He retooled. He rebranded. And he returned to the people.
"Linda Mwananchi" was not born in a boardroom. It was forged in the markets of Kakamega, in the border towns of Busia, in the sugarcane fields where farmers watched their livelihoods wither, and in the homes of Kenyans struggling to navigate the complexities of the Social Health Authority's healthcare rollout. Sifuna's grassroots tours across Western Kenya became more than political excursions; they became pilgrimages.
The movement zeroed in on the issues that mattered to ordinary Kenyans: the controversial SHA rollout that left many confused and uncovered; government housing programs that seemed to prioritize optics over affordability; and the dying sugar sector, once the backbone of Western Kenya's economy, now gasping under the weight of neglect and mismanagement.
But "Linda Mwananchi" was more than a critique. It was a declaration. For the Luhya community, long consigned to the role of kingmakers and deputy presidents, Sifuna's message was revolutionary: No more. The community would no longer settle for second place. The top seat was not just aspirational it was attainable. And Sifuna, with his legal mind and oratorical gifts, intended to be the one to claim it.

The 2027 Horizon

The presidential bid was not announced with the fanfare of a traditional political declaration. It emerged organically, like a river finding its course. Sifuna's grassroots mobilization campaign has been methodical, deliberate, and unmistakably ambitious. While others have relied on party machinery and deep-pocketed financiers, Sifuna has turned to something far more democratic: the people themselves.
His campaigns have been funded through public crowdfunding, popular paybill drives that allow ordinary Kenyans to buy into the movement with whatever they can afford. It is a radical reimagining of political financing in Kenya, where campaigns have historically been the playground of the wealthy elite. In Sifuna's model, every contribution is a stake, every donor a shareholder in the dream of a different kind of presidency.
The political mathematics are equally fascinating. Wiper Party Leader Kalonzo Musyoka, a veteran of Kenyan politics and a man who has himself eyed the presidency, made a stunning declaration: he would be willing to deputize Sifuna if it meant forging a united opposition front capable of defeating the current administration. For a politician of Kalonzo's stature to offer the deputy slot to a relative newcomer speaks volumes about the gravitational pull Sifuna has generated in Kenya's opposition space.

Sisi Ndio Sifuna: The Digital Insurgency

If "Linda Mwananchi" is the soul of Sifuna's movement, then "Sisi Ndio Sifuna" is its heartbeat in the digital realm.
On TikTok and X (formerly Twitter), a generation of Kenyans who have historically been dismissed as politically apathetic have found their champion. Sifuna's appeal to Gen Z and the youth is not manufactured; it is earned. He speaks their language, engages with their memes, and addresses their anxieties about unemployment, housing, and a future that often feels precarious.
His fiery, articulate style translates perfectly to the short-form, high-energy nature of social media. A Sifuna clip can move from a blistering critique of government policy to a witty takedown of a political opponent to an impassioned plea for national unity all in under sixty seconds. The youth have responded not as passive consumers but as active co-creators, generating content, organizing online, and amplifying the "Sisi Ndio Sifuna" wave into a cultural phenomenon.
This is not astroturfing. It is organic, decentralized, and powerful. In a country where the median age is below twenty, capturing the youth is not just good politics, it is survival.

The Advocate's Dilemma

Yet for all the momentum, the road to State House is paved with contradictions. Sifuna is a man caught between identities: the polished advocate who understands the establishment, and the populist firebrand who has pledged to dismantle it. The seasoned party operative who knows where the bodies are buried, and the outsider who promises to bury the old order. The Luhya son who carries the hopes of a community, and the national leader who must convince forty-seven counties that his vision transcends ethnicity.
His legal background is both asset and anchor. It gives him credibility, discipline, and strategic patience. But politics, especially Kenyan politics, often rewards the theatrical over the substantive, the emotional over the evidentiary. Sifuna's challenge is to maintain his intellectual rigor while wielding the emotional resonance that moves masses.
The crowdfunding model, revolutionary as it is, faces its own tests. Can a presidential campaign be sustained on small donations in a political economy dominated by deep-state interests and corporate largesse? Will the paybill drives generate the hundreds of millions required for a national campaign, or will Sifuna eventually be forced to make the kind of alliances that have compromised every Kenyan politician before him?
posts.author: Hamisi Ogula

posts.title: Parliament Debates Bill to Enforce Strict 30-Day KUCCPS Placement Timelines
posts.excerpt: The proposed Tertiary Education, Placement, and Funding Bill, 2026, would compel the placement agency to open applications within 30 days of KCSE results, process them within a month, and allow unsuccessful students to revise their choices at no cost as Kenya moves toward 100% university funding.
posts.content:
Kenyan lawmakers are currently deliberating on legislation that would impose rigid deadlines on the Kenya Universities and Colleges Central Placement Service (KUCCPS) regarding how quickly it manages student admissions to tertiary institutions.
The proposed Tertiary Education, Placement, and Funding Bill, 2026, would mandate that KUCCPS begin accepting placement applications no later than one month following the announcement of national examination outcomes. This marks a significant acceleration compared to existing practice; for example, in 2026 the agency only opened its application portal three months after KCSE results were declared.
Under the new legal framework, the placement body would also be required to complete the evaluation of all submitted applications within a 30-day window and subsequently notify both the students and the respective institutions of their decisions.
The legislation aims to elevate KUCCPS into an independent statutory authority with sole responsibility for coordinating student admissions across universities and colleges. Additionally, applicants who fail to secure placement in their chosen programs would be permitted to select alternative courses without incurring any revision charges. These students would be given a fortnight to submit revised preferences. Meanwhile, candidates who missed the original application period would be afforded another opportunity to apply, though they would be subject to the standard application fee. KUCCPS would then have 15 days to finalize decisions on both revised and late applications.
The Bill further obligates public universities and colleges to furnish KUCCPS with comprehensive details about their intended academic programs, enrollment capacities, and approved tuition fees at least two months prior to the release of national exam results. KUCCPS would then verify this data alongside relevant regulatory agencies and make it publicly accessible through its online platform, enabling prospective students to make informed decisions based on actual course availability and costs.
These reforms align with the government's broader initiative to implement fully subsidized university education for all qualifying students beginning September 2026.
posts.author: Hamisi Ogula

posts.title: President Ruto Consolidates Kenya Kwanza-ODM Coalition, Launches Vision 2060 and Elders' Stipend Package
posts.excerpt: President William Ruto has formalized a broad-based political alliance with ODM ahead of the 2027 election, opened nationwide consultations for Kenya Vision 2060, and announced a Ksh 3,000 monthly stipend for 106,000 village elders even as former Deputy Rigathi Gachagua escalates criticism over the Sh13.02 trillion national debt.
posts.content:
President Ruto Consolidates Kenya Kwanza-ODM Coalition, Launches Vision 2060 and Elders' Stipend Package

President William Ruto has formalized a broad-based political alliance with ODM ahead of the 2027 election, opened nationwide consultations for Kenya Vision 2060, and announced a Ksh 3,000 monthly stipend for 106,000 village elders—even as former Deputy Rigathi Gachagua escalates criticism over the Sh13.02 trillion national debt.
Nairobi, Kenya — President William Ruto is moving aggressively to reshape Kenya’s political and economic landscape just months before the 2027 General Election, anchoring his strategy on a historic coalition with the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), a long-term development blueprint, and fresh social support for traditional leaders.
The fifth President of Kenya, who assumed office on September 13, 2022, after serving as the country’s first elected Deputy President from 2013 to 2022, is leveraging his Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA) to drive a narrative of continuity and structural reform. However, his administration remains under intense scrutiny over rising national debt and a bruising public fallout with his former deputy.

Kenya Kwanza-ODM Alliance Takes Shape

In what political analysts are calling one of the most significant realignments in recent Kenyan history, President Ruto has formalized a broad-based coalition between his ruling Kenya Kwanza alliance and ODM, the party long associated with opposition leader Raila Odinga.
The partnership was cemented during a high-profile, three-day retreat in Naivasha, where Ruto chaired deliberations alongside Oburu Oginga.
A key ODM leader and elder statesman. The retreat focused on structuring the framework of the alliance, which is widely seen as an effort to consolidate power and neutralize opposition ahead of the 2027 polls.
The move has sent shockwaves through Kenya’s political establishment, with critics arguing that the merger blurs the line between government and opposition, while supporters maintain it is necessary for national stability and legislative efficiency.
Gachagua’s Counter-Offensive
The coalition-building comes as President Ruto faces sustained attacks from his former Deputy President, Rigathi Gachagua, who has emerged as one of the administration’s most vocal critics.
In a recent lengthy public address, Gachagua hit out at Ruto’s economic choices, specifically questioning the administration’s appetite for national borrowing and the sustainability of its fiscal policies. The former DP accused the government of mortgaging Kenya’s future, a charge that has resonated with segments of the public feeling the pinch of a high cost of living.
Presidential allies have, however, vigorously countered Gachagua’s claims, accusing the former deputy of inciting division and peddling revisionist narratives. The public spat has exposed deepening rifts within the Kenya Kwanza camp, raising questions about whether Gachagua will mount a serious challenge in 2027 or remain a spoiler from the sidelines.
Vision 2060: Thinking Beyond the Next Election
Amid the political maneuvering, President Ruto is attempting to pivot the national conversation toward long-term planning. On Wednesday, he officially opened nationwide public consultations for Kenya Vision 2060 at the Kenyatta International Convention Centre (KICC) in Nairobi.
The launch of the post-Vision 2030 blueprint has drawn both praise and skepticism, with critics questioning the timing of such an ambitious long-term plan less than a year before a high-stakes election. But Ruto defended the early rollout, urging Kenyans to “think about the next generation, not the next election.”
Vision 2060 is expected to guide Kenya’s development trajectory for the next three decades, with focus areas likely to include digital transformation, climate resilience, manufacturing, and human capital development. The nationwide consultations are designed to crowdsource input from citizens, county governments, and private sector stakeholders.
Ksh 3,000 Monthly Stipend for Village Elders
In a move that blends social policy with grassroots political mobilization, President Ruto announced a formal national recognition package for over 106,000 village elders across Kenya.
The package includes:
  • A Ksh 3,000 monthly stipend
  • Smartphones for digital connectivity
  • Leadership training
  • Formal healthcare coverage through the Social Health Authority (SHA)
The announcement signals the administration’s recognition of the role traditional elders play in dispute resolution, community cohesion, and local governance. It also comes at a time when the SHA rollout remains under public scrutiny, with critics questioning its implementation and affordability.
Debt and Economic Pressures
Despite the headline-grabbing initiatives, President Ruto’s administration continues to walk an economic tightrope. Kenya’s national debt currently stands at approximately Sh13.02 trillion, a figure that has fueled public anxiety and provided ammunition for opposition figures like Gachagua.
While the government has defended its borrowing as necessary to finance critical infrastructure expansion, economists and civil society groups have warned that debt servicing is consuming an unsustainable portion of national revenue, crowding out spending on health, education, and social services.
Infrastructure projects initiated under Ruto’s watch continue to advance, but the administration faces the delicate task of balancing development spending with fiscal responsibility in an increasingly skeptical political environment.
What’s Next?
With the 2027 General Election inching closer, President Ruto appears to be executing a multi-pronged strategy: neutralize opposition through co-option, secure the grassroots through tangible benefits, and project statesmanship through long-term planning. Whether this formula can withstand the dual pressures of economic hardship and political betrayal remains the defining question of his first term.
For now, the Kenya Kwanza-ODM axis, Vision 2060, and the village elders’ package have given the President a busy news cycle and plenty of material for both supporters and detractors to debate.
posts.author: Hamisi Ogula

posts.title: Jaramogi Mausoleum Closed for Three Months as KDF Begins Raila Odinga Memorial Construction in Bondo
posts.excerpt: The National Museums of Kenya has shut the Jaramogi Oginga Odinga Mausoleum until October 30, 2026, to allow the Kenya Defence Forces to construct a pentagonal memorial for the late Prime Minister Raila Odinga featuring a research center, library, and amphitheater at a cost of Ksh30 million.
posts.content:
The National Museums of Kenya (NMK) has announced that the Jaramogi Oginga Odinga Mausoleum in Bondo, Siaya County, will remain closed to the public for three months to facilitate major construction works at the heritage site.
In a statement issued on Wednesday, NMK confirmed that the facility was shut on Monday, July 20, and will not reopen until Friday, October 30. Members of the public and tourists have been urged to avoid the site during this period, as no visitors will be granted access until the construction is fully completed.
The closure clears the way for the building of the Raila Odinga mausoleum, a permanent memorial dedicated to the late former Prime Minister. The Kenya Defence Forces (KDF) is carrying out the construction, which is scheduled for completion by the end of October.
The government, through the Ministry of Culture, had previously released Ksh30 million to fund both the new Raila memorial and the renovation of the existing Jaramogi mausoleum.
Architecturally, the new Raila Mausoleum will adopt a pentagonal design, distinguishing it from the hexagonal Jaramogi Mausoleum erected in 1995. The five-sided structure is meant to symbolize strength, unity, and collective purpose.
Once finished, the complex will house a research center, a library, digital archives, and an amphitheater, with NMK set to participate in managing the facilities.
The Bondo site remains a key destination for visitors interested in Kenya’s political, cultural history and continues to fall under the stewardship of the National Museums of Kenya.
posts.author: Hamisi Yusuf

posts.title: Rigathi Gachagua Leads Opposition from DCP, Demands Answers on Raila Death as DCI Calls for Evidence.
posts.excerpt:
Impeached Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has reinvented himself as a fierce government critic through his Democracy for the Citizens Party, sparking national controversy with claims about Raila Odinga’s death, prompting the DCI and allies like Junet Mohammed to demand proof while challenging his record in office.
.
posts.content:
Nairobi, Kenya — Nearly two years after his historic impeachment from the Office of the Deputy President in October 2024, Rigathi Gachagua has completed a dramatic political reinvention. Once the second-in-command in President William Ruto’s Kenya Kwanza administration, Gachagua now leads the Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP), from where he has emerged as one of the government’s most relentless and outspoken critics.
His impeachment, making him the first Deputy President in Kenya’s history to be removed through that process—would have ended the careers of lesser politicians. Instead, Gachagua has weaponized his ouster into a rallying cry, positioning himself as a victim of political betrayal and a defender of the marginalized.
From Civil Servant to Deputy President to Opposition Leader
Gachagua’s journey through Kenya’s public life spans decades. A graduate of the University of Nairobi (Class of 1988) with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and Literature, he cut his teeth in student politics as the leader of the Nyeri District University Students Association. He also holds an Advanced Diploma in Public Administration.
His civil service career began as a District Officer, rising through the ranks to serve as Assistant Secretary in the Ministry of Home Affairs and National Heritage, and later as a personal assistant to then-Cabinet Minister Uhuru Kenyatta and subsequently to the Head of the Public Service. Before his elevation to the Deputy Presidency in 2022, he represented Mathira Constituency in the National Assembly from 2017 to 2022.
Following his impeachment, Kithure Kindiki was appointed to replace him. But Gachagua refused to fade into political obscurity.
The Raila Odinga Death Controversy
Gachagua’s latest firestorm involves the death of opposition leader Raila Odinga. In recent days, he has publicly demanded answers regarding the circumstances of Raila’s death a move that has drawn sharp rebuke from across the political spectrum.
Junet Mohammed, the Suna East MP and longtime Raila ally, slammed Gachagua for his comments, noting that the former Deputy President had not publicly mourned Raila or visited his family after his passing. Junet accused Gachagua of exploiting tragedy for political mileage.
The Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) has also weighed in, telling Gachagua to “bring credible evidence, not claims.” The law enforcement agency’s blunt message signals growing official impatience with Gachagua’s rhetoric, raising the stakes in his confrontation with the state.
Allies Hit Back
National Assembly Majority Leader Kimani Ichung’wah has openly challenged Gachagua to list his record as Deputy President rather than engage in what Ichung’wah characterizes as divisive and baseless attacks. The exchange underscores the bitterness that still defines the relationship between Gachagua and his former Kenya Kwanza allies.
Personal Life
Away from the political theater, Gachagua is married to Pastor Dorcas Rigathi. The couple has two sons.
posts.author: Hamisi Ogula

posts.title: Julia Ojiambo: Kenya’s First Female Presidential Candidate, Pioneer MP and Nutrition Professor Who Shattered the Glass Ceiling
posts.excerpt: From becoming the first African woman admitted to the Royal Technical College in 1956 to founding Maendeleo ya Wanawake and running as Kenya’s first female presidential aspirant, Julia Auma Ojiambo’s eight-decade journey has redefined women’s roles in politics, academia, and public health.
posts.content:
Julia Auma Ojiambo stands as one of Kenya’s most consequential women leaders, having spent nearly nine decades breaking barriers across education, research, activism, and elective politics. Born on 29 November 1936 in what is now Busia County to pioneer African missionaries, she was among the first eight beneficiaries of the African Girls High School pilot project, later earning her Cambridge School Certificate in 1954 at the age of 17.
Her academic path was defined by a series of historic firsts. The Ministry of Education posted her to Friends School Kamusinga under a USAID-backed pilot programme introducing agricultural studies in secondary schools, before transferring her to Vihiga Teachers College to upgrade teachers from P4 to P3. On 26 April 1956, barely a year after finishing high school, she was admitted as the first African female student at the Royal Technical College, now the University of Nairobi where she studied at the Home Science Department and graduated with a Diploma in Home Economics in 1958.
A United Nations/FAO/UNICEF fellowship took her to London University, where she earned a Bachelor’s Degree in Community Health and briefly served as a broadcaster for the BBC World Service’s East African channel. Upon returning to Kenya, she became the first African woman appointed as an Assistant Lecturer and the first African woman warden at the University of Nairobi. She also chaired the Kenya Housewives Consumer Organization, which she transformed into the Kenya Consumers Organization.
Further scholarships enabled her to pursue a Master of Science in Public Health at Harvard University and later enroll in a PhD programme at McGill University in Canada. Family commitments, however, led her to complete her doctorate at the University of Nairobi’s new Medical School, making her the first student to obtain a PhD from that faculty. She went on to lecture at both the University of Nairobi and Kenyatta University and currently holds the rank of Professor in Nutrition.
Deeply affected by systemic gender inequality, Ojiambo founded the Centre for the Advancement of Women and Children, an NGO focused on grassroots civic education and human rights awareness. She was also a founding member of the Maendeleo ya Wanawake Organization (MYWO), the umbrella women’s empowerment group with nationwide reach. While studying in London, she represented Kenya at the All-Country Women of the World Conference at the Royal Albert Hall as a MYWO delegate.
Her advocacy peaked during the UN Decade for Women (1976–1985). She attended the 1975 Mexico conference and the 1980 Copenhagen forum and notably led the Kenyan delegation at the landmark 1985 Nairobi conference despite not holding parliamentary office at the time. She was also instrumental in Kenya’s participation at the 1995 Beijing conference.
Ojiambo’s entry into politics was bruising. She was physically assaulted, threatened with sexual violence, and smeared as a prostitute for daring to contest parliamentary seats in 1979 and beyond experiences that only hardened her resolve to fight for affirmative action. She became a central figure in Kenya’s National Gender Machinery, which later secured constitutional gains including the one-third gender rule, the Affirmative Action Bill, and the Political Parties Act of 2011.
In 1974, she made history by winning the Busia Central parliamentary seat against Arthur Ochwada a former freedom fighter with close ties to the first family through marriage becoming only the second black woman in Kenya to defeat a male opponent after Grace Onyango. She served until 1978 and was appointed Kenya’s first female Assistant Minister for Housing and Social Services. After Moi succeeded Kenyatta, she reclaimed a seat in 1979, this time winning the Funyula constituency with overwhelming support from women voters. Her second term was cut short by the 1982 attempted coup, which triggered an emergency election in 1983 that saw Moody Awori succeed her.
In Parliament, she championed legislation that led to the creation of the Kenya Nutritionists and Dieticians Institute (KNDI). She later served as Assistant Minister for Basic Education in 1982.
Her party-political journey mirrored Kenya’s shifting landscape. She began as a KANU member, serving as the party’s director of Youth and Women Affairs and establishing the controversial Youth for KANU ’92 wing. As multi-party politics took hold, she defected to Ford Kenya before forming the Labour Party of Kenya (LPK), becoming its first female chairperson.
Ahead of the 2007 elections, LPK joined the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) coalition. When the coalition fractured, Ojiambo sided with Kalonzo Musyoka in the ODM-K splinter group. Both declared presidential ambitions, but she was ousted during party nominations. She ultimately ran as Kalonzo’s running mate in the volatile 2007 contest, which they lost. Kalonzo’s failure to nominate her to Parliament afterwards marked the collapse of their political alliance.
Today, Julia Ojiambo remains a towering symbol of resilience, a nutrition professor, a gender rights architect, and the first woman in Kenya’s history to declare a presidential bid.
posts.author: Hamisi Ogula

posts.title: Orengo, Babu Owino Allege State-Funded Plot to Disrupt Linda Mwananchi Rally in Homa Bay
posts.excerpt: Siaya Governor and Embakasi East MP claim intelligence shows youths are being armed and mobilized to attack the August 16 gathering, with meetings allegedly held to coordinate the violence.
posts.content:
Siaya Governor James Orengo and Embakasi East MP Babu Owino have raised alarm over what they describe as an orchestrated plan to unleash violence at the upcoming Linda Mwananchi rally set for August 16 in Homa Bay County.
Addressing the media on Wednesday, the leaders claimed they had obtained intelligence suggesting that young people were being organized and equipped with crude weapons such as clubs, machetes, and knives to disrupt the event. Orengo asserted that he was the primary target of the alleged scheme, which he said was being bankrolled by the state through local politicians from Homa Bay.
Suba South MP Caroli Omondi elaborated on the claims, stating that a planning meeting had reportedly taken place at Genoa Center in Homa Bay Town. According to Omondi, the alleged plotters intended to position youths near Kabunde Airstrip under the pretense of conducting voter registration, with the real aim of blocking access routes into the town and preventing rally attendees from reaching the venue. He added that the movement had secured audio recordings from these alleged planning sessions and had forwarded them to security agencies.
The leaders have formally written to the Interior Ministry and the National Police Service requesting protection for the event. Despite the threats, they vowed that the rally would go ahead as scheduled, insisting that their constitutional rights to assembly and political association must be upheld.
The warnings come against a backdrop of recent violent incidents involving Linda Mwananchi members. In May 2026, Orengo’s motorcade was attacked during a tour of Homa Bay, resulting in damaged vehicles. In early July, a convoy in Keumbu, Kisii County, was pelted with stones in an attack that left one person dead and over 20 injured. Shortly afterward, armed youths reportedly tried to interrupt a church service attended by Orengo and Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna in Kisumu. The movement also cited a recent assault on its Homa Bay County coordinator, lawyer Samwel Nyauke, as part of a broader pattern of intimidation.
Government and police officials have repeatedly denied any involvement in sponsoring political violence.
posts.author: Hamisi Yusuf

posts.title: Lakers Sold for Record $12.5 Billion to Josh Kushner and Bob Iger Just a Year After Previous Sale
posts.excerpt: Venture capitalist Josh Kushner and former Disney CEO Bob Iger are set to take over the iconic NBA franchise from Mark Walter, who purchased it for $10 billion only last June.
posts.content:
The Los Angeles Lakers are changing hands once again, this time in a historic $12.5 billion deal that shatters the record for the most expensive sale of a sports franchise anywhere in the world.
The buyers are a group led by venture capitalist Josh Kushner and former Walt Disney Company CEO Bob Iger. The pair, who had reportedly been involved in efforts to secure an NBA expansion team in Las Vegas, pivoted to acquire the Lakers after approaching current owner Mark Walter with an offer last Sunday.
Walter, who also owns the Los Angeles Dodgers, had bought a controlling stake in the Lakers from the Buss family for $10 billion in June 2025, and then it was its own record. His brief tenure as Lakers owner is now ending with a staggering $2.5 billion profit in just over a year.
In a joint statement, Kushner and Iger expressed deep respect for the franchise's legacy. "As lifelong NBA fans, we are deeply honored for the opportunity to become stewards of the Los Angeles Lakers, one of the most iconic sports franchises in the world. We have immense respect for the leadership and vision of Jerry and Jeanie Buss," they said. "Our long-term commitment is to build on that foundation, compete at the highest level, and serve this extraordinary team, its fans, and the city of Los Angeles."
Iger confirmed that the new ownership group intends to honor the existing agreement that keeps Jeanie Buss as the Lakers' governor for the next five years.
Despite selling the Lakers, Walter is expected to retain ownership of the Dodgers. His decision to sell comes as he faces a federal probe into whether he properly disclosed loans tied to his companies, though the investigation has not been cited as a reason for the sale.
Kushner, the brother of Jared Kushner, son-in-law to U.S. President Donald Trump, already holds minority stakes in the Memphis Grizzlies and Miami Heat, both of which he would be required to divest under NBA ownership rules.
The Lakers' most celebrated legend, Magic Johnson, publicly endorsed the sale on social media, signaling his support for Iger's involvement.
The franchise is coming off a 53-29 season that ended in the Western Conference semifinals. However, the offseason was rocked by LeBron James's departure to the Philadelphia 76ers on a two-year contract, leaving Luka Dončić as the team's centerpiece.
The deal values the Lakers at nearly 185 times what Jerry Buss paid for the team in 1979 ($67.5 million), cementing the franchise as not just basketball royalty but one of the most valuable properties in all of global sports.
